lead: Power cycles turn heat into work; refrigeration cycles spend work or heat to move heat from a cold place to a hot one. This unit shows how to sketch each cycle, fix its states, and compute its efficiency, work, mean effective pressure and COP from air or steam tables. After it you can analyse an Otto, Diesel, Dual, Brayton, Stirling, Rankine, reheat, regenerative, vapour compression or vapour absorption cycle from a given set of pressures and temperatures.
about: The unit turns the laws of thermodynamics into numbers for real machines. Chapter 6.1 fixes the four assumptions that let an engine be analysed as a closed loop of air. Chapters 6.2 and 6.3 give the shapes of the Otto, Diesel, Dual, Brayton and Stirling cycles. Chapter 6.4 reduces every gas cycle to two numbers, air standard efficiency and mean effective pressure, and compares them on a stated basis. Chapter 6.5 moves to steam, where the fluid changes phase and the Rankine cycle replaces the gas cycle. Chapter 6.6 adds reheat and regeneration to it. Chapter 6.7 runs the cycle backwards for cooling, and 6.8 replaces the compressor with a heat-driven generator. Every chapter answers the same question: how much work or cooling per unit of heat supplied.

chapters.idea: Replace the real engine with a closed loop of ideal air, so that the whole cycle can be worked out from four simple reversible processes.
chapters.depth: Cover the four standard assumptions one by one: a fixed mass of air behaving as an ideal gas with constant specific heats (γ = 1.4, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K); heat added from an external source so no fuel, combustion or exhaust gas appears; all processes internally reversible; the cycle closes with heat rejected to a sink at constant volume. Show the Carnot cycle as the reference (two isotherms, two isentropics) on p-v and T-s, and say why plants do not use it: isothermal heat transfer at high speed is impossible, pressures become enormous, and net work per cycle is small. Define air standard efficiency as η = w_net/q_in. Some syllabi call these the ideal cycle assumptions or the cold air standard assumptions.

figure.aria: A tree of the four air standard assumptions, each branching into its two sub-conditions, with the closed cycle as the fourth branch.

chapters.example: Air at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed isentropically through a volume ratio of 8 in an air standard cycle. Take γ = 1.4 and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. Find the pressure and temperature after compression, and name the assumption that allows you to use pv^1.4 = constant. Answer: p2 = p1 × 8^1.4 = 1 × 18.38 = 18.4 bar; T2 = T1 × 8^0.4 = 300 × 2.297 = 689 K. The reversibility assumption gives pv^γ = constant; the ideal gas assumption with constant γ gives the value 1.4.
chapters.trap: Treating the air standard efficiency as the brake efficiency of a real engine. It is an upper bound that ignores friction, heat loss, incomplete combustion and the changing γ of hot exhaust gas.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (work, heat and sign convention); Unit 3 (Carnot cycle and Carnot efficiency).
chapters.leave: Steam properties and dryness fraction to Unit 5; exergy and second law efficiency of cycles to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: How the heat is added, at constant volume, at constant pressure, or partly both, fixes the shape of the cycle and its efficiency formula.
chapters.depth: Otto cycle: 1-2 isentropic compression, 2-3 constant volume heat addition, 3-4 isentropic expansion, 4-1 constant volume heat rejection. Compression ratio r = v1/v2 = v4/v3, T2/T1 = r^(γ-1), η = 1 - 1/r^(γ-1). Diesel cycle: heat added at constant pressure, cutoff ratio rc = v3/v2 = T3/T2, η = 1 - (1/r^(γ-1))·(rc^γ - 1)/(γ(rc - 1)). Dual cycle: rp = p3/p2 for the constant volume part and rc = v4/v3 for the constant pressure part, η = 1 - (1/r^(γ-1))·(rp·rc^γ - 1)/((rp - 1) + γ·rp·(rc - 1)). Derive each from q_in - q_out, and draw p-v and T-s for all three. Some syllabi call the Dual cycle the mixed cycle or the limited pressure cycle.

figure.aria: A p-v plot of the Otto cycle 1-2-3-4-1, with isentropic compression and expansion and two vertical constant volume lines.

chapters.example: An air standard Otto cycle has compression ratio 8. Air enters at 1 bar and 300 K. Heat added is 800 kJ/kg. Take cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find T2, T3, T4, the air standard efficiency, the net work and the heat rejected. Answer: T2 = 300 × 8^0.4 = 689.1 K. T3 = T2 + q_in/cv = 689.1 + 800/0.718 = 1803.3 K. T4 = T3/8^0.4 = 1803.3/2.297 = 784.9 K. η = 1 - 1/2.297 = 0.565. q_out = 0.718 × (784.9 - 300) = 348.2 kJ/kg. w_net = 800 - 348.2 = 451.8 kJ/kg, and 451.8/800 = 0.565, as it must. p3 = p2 × T3/T2 = 18.4 × 2.62 = 48.1 bar.
chapters.trap: Swapping the compression ratio r = v1/v2 with the cutoff ratio rc = v3/v2, and using cv for the constant pressure heat addition of the Diesel cycle.
chapters.leave: Mean effective pressure and the comparison of the three cycles to Chapter 6.4.

chapters.idea: A gas turbine is the same four processes as Otto, but steady flow makes the pressure ratio the key variable; Stirling uses two isotherms and a regenerator instead.
chapters.depth: Brayton cycle: compressor 1-2, heater 2-3, turbine 3-4, cooler 4-1, all heat transfer at constant pressure. Pressure ratio rp = p2/p1, T2/T1 = T3/T4 = rp^((γ-1)/γ), η = 1 - 1/rp^((γ-1)/γ). Define back work ratio w_c/w_t and the specific work w_t - w_c. Mention the regenerator in one line and the open gas turbine (fresh air, fuel, exhaust) against the closed cycle. Stirling cycle: two isotherms and two constant volume processes, with a regenerator that stores and returns heat; its ideal efficiency equals the Carnot value between the same two temperatures. Say why it needs an external heat source and a good regenerator. Some syllabi call Brayton the Joule cycle or the constant pressure cycle.

figure.title: Brayton cycle
figure.aria: Four blocks in a closed loop: compressor, heater, turbine and cooler, with state numbers 1 to 4 on the connecting lines.

chapters.example: A Brayton cycle has pressure ratio 8, compressor inlet 300 K and turbine inlet 1200 K. Take cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find the four temperatures, the net work and the efficiency. Answer: 8^((1.4-1)/1.4) = 8^0.2857 = 1.811. T2 = 300 × 1.811 = 543.4 K; T4 = 1200/1.811 = 662.5 K. w_c = 1.005 × (543.4 - 300) = 244.6 kJ/kg; w_t = 1.005 × (1200 - 662.5) = 540.2 kJ/kg; w_net = 295.6 kJ/kg. q_in = 1.005 × (1200 - 543.4) = 659.9 kJ/kg. η = 295.6/659.9 = 0.448 = 1 - 1/1.811.
chapters.trap: Using a volume ratio inside a steady flow cycle, and expecting the efficiency to rise when the turbine inlet temperature is raised. At fixed rp the efficiency stays the same; only the specific work grows.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 and 6.2; Unit 2 (steady flow energy equation).
chapters.leave: Regenerator effectiveness and gas turbine blade cooling to later courses; the comparison of gas and steam plants to Chapter 6.5.

chapters.idea: Two numbers compare every gas cycle: the air standard efficiency from the temperatures, and the mean effective pressure from the net work and the swept volume.
chapters.depth: Define air standard efficiency, specific work (kJ/kg), work ratio and mean effective pressure MEP = w_net/(v1 - v2), where v1 - v2 is the swept volume per kg. Units: kJ/kg ÷ m³/kg gives kPa, so divide by 100 for bar. Compare the cycles at the same compression ratio (Otto highest, then Dual, then Diesel) and at the same maximum pressure and temperature (Diesel highest, then Dual, then Otto). Explain why: constant volume heat addition raises the mean temperature of heat supply more. Add the effect of γ, of r and of rc, and the practical limits — knock limits r in petrol engines, peak pressure and rate of pressure rise limit rc in diesel engines.

figure.aria: Three efficiency curves rising with compression ratio, with Otto highest, Dual in the middle and Diesel lowest at the same compression ratio.

chapters.example: For the Otto cycle of Chapter 6.2 (r = 8, p1 = 1 bar, T1 = 300 K, w_net = 451.8 kJ/kg), find the specific volume at the start and end of compression and the mean effective pressure. Answer: v1 = RT1/p1 = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³/kg (p in kPa). v2 = v1/8 = 0.1076 m³/kg. MEP = 451.8/(0.861 - 0.1076) = 451.8/0.7534 = 599.7 kPa ≈ 6.0 bar.
chapters.trap: Dividing the net work by v1 instead of the swept volume v1 - v2, and giving the cycle comparison without saying whether r or the maximum pressure and temperature is held the same.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 6.1 to 6.3; Unit 1 (displacement work, p-v area).
chapters.leave: Knock and combustion details to the IC engines course; actual indicator diagrams to the laboratory.

chapters.idea: A steam plant is a Rankine cycle: pump, boiler, turbine and condenser, with a pump that compresses liquid instead of a compressor that must handle a two-phase mixture.
chapters.depth: The four processes with the plant parts named, on T-s and h-s. Explain why a Carnot cycle with steam is impractical: the compression would start inside the dome, a compressor handling wet steam is bulky and damage prone, and the work per cycle is small. Pump work ≈ vf(P2 - P1) with vf in m³/kg and P in kPa, giving kJ/kg. Thermal efficiency η = (w_t - w_p)/q_in with q_in = h3 - h2. Read every state from the steam tables, using s3 = s4 inside the dome to get the dryness x4. Then the three knobs: raise boiler pressure (η up, x4 down), lower condenser pressure (η up, limited by cooling water temperature), superheat (η up and x4 up). Show that this triangle of effects is what forces reheat and regeneration. Some syllabi call this the simple ideal Rankine cycle.

figure.title: Rankine cycle
figure.aria: Four blocks in a loop: pump, boiler, turbine and condenser, with state numbers showing steam leaving the boiler and wet steam leaving the turbine.

chapters.example: Steam at 40 bar and 400 °C enters a turbine and expands to 0.1 bar, is condensed and pumped back. From tables: h3 = 3213.6 kJ/kg, s3 = 6.7690 kJ/kg·K; at 0.1 bar, hf = 191.8, hfg = 2392.8, sf = 0.6493, sfg = 7.5009 kJ/kg·K, vf = 0.001010 m³/kg. Find the exhaust dryness, the works and the cycle efficiency. Answer: x4 = (6.7690 - 0.6493)/7.5009 = 0.816. h4 = 191.8 + 0.816 × 2392.8 = 2144.0 kJ/kg. w_t = 3213.6 - 2144.0 = 1069.6 kJ/kg. w_p = 0.001010 × (4000 - 10) = 4.0 kJ/kg. h1 = 191.8 + 4.0 = 195.8 kJ/kg. q_in = 3213.6 - 195.8 = 3017.8 kJ/kg. η = (1069.6 - 4.0)/3017.8 = 0.353, about 35.3 %.
chapters.trap: Getting the pump work wrong in size or sign (P2 - P1 must be in kPa), and taking the enthalpy after the pump as hf at condenser pressure instead of hf plus pump work.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 (steam tables, dryness fraction, superheated steam); Unit 3 (T-s diagram).
chapters.leave: Boiler efficiency, condenser design and feedwater treatment to the power plant course.

chapters.idea: Reheat removes the wetness that high boiler pressure creates; regeneration takes heat from the steam itself to warm the feedwater, raising the mean temperature of heat addition.
chapters.depth: Reheat: expand in the HP turbine to an intermediate pressure, return the whole flow to the reheater, then expand in the LP turbine. Work and heat both rise; efficiency rises only slightly but the exhaust dryness rises a lot. State the rule of thumb that the best reheat pressure is roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the boiler pressure. Regeneration: bleed a fraction of the steam from the turbine to heat the feedwater; open feed heater (direct contact mixing chamber, one heater at a time) and closed feed heater (surface exchanger, drains cascaded back to the next heater or the condenser). Explain the accounting: bled steam produces no work below the bleed point, so work falls, but the boiler heat input falls more because the feedwater enters warmer. Sketch the plant layout for one bleed and one reheater.

figure.title: Reheat Rankine
figure.aria: A loop of boiler, high pressure turbine, reheater, low pressure turbine, condenser and pump, with steam returning from the reheater to the low pressure turbine.

chapters.example: Use the plant of Chapter 6.5 but reheat from 40 bar to 4 bar and back to 400 °C. Tables give h4 = 2685.6 kJ/kg (x = 0.975 at 4 bar) and h5 = 3273.9 kJ/kg, s5 = 7.8985 kJ/kg·K; at 0.1 bar x6 = (7.8985 - 0.6493)/7.5009 = 0.966, h6 = 191.8 + 0.966 × 2392.8 = 2504.2 kJ/kg. Answer: w_t = (3213.6 - 2685.6) + (3273.9 - 2504.2) = 528.0 + 769.7 = 1297.7 kJ/kg. w_net = 1297.7 - 4.0 = 1293.7 kJ/kg. q_in = (3213.6 - 195.8) + (3273.9 - 2685.6) = 3017.8 + 588.3 = 3606.1 kJ/kg. η = 1293.7/3606.1 = 0.359. The efficiency moves from 35.3 % to 35.9 %, but the exhaust dryness moves from 0.816 to 0.966, which is the real gain.
chapters.trap: Adding the reheater heat to the boiler heat twice or leaving it out, and forgetting that bled steam does no work below the bleed point, so the bleed fraction must be found before the work is summed.
chapters.leave: Detailed heater design, drain cooler sizing and plant heat rate to the power plant course.

chapters.idea: A refrigerator is the Rankine cycle run backwards: a throttle drops the pressure at constant enthalpy, and the evaporator takes heat in at a low temperature.
chapters.depth: Four components: evaporator, compressor, condenser, expansion valve. Show the cycle on p-h and T-s. Stress that the expansion valve is isenthalpic, h4 = h3, so the process is a vertical line on p-h and a curve inside the dome on T-s. Refrigeration effect = h1 - h4, compressor work = h2 - h1, COP = (h1 - h4)/(h2 - h1). Give the Carnot COP = TL/(TH - TL) between the same two temperatures as the upper bound and explain why the real cycle falls short (throttling, superheated suction, pressure drops). One tonne of refrigeration = 3.5 kW; mass flow = duty/refrigeration effect. Effects in one line each: raising evaporator pressure raises COP; lowering condenser pressure raises COP; suction superheat protects the compressor but costs COP; liquid subcooling gains COP. Name common refrigerants: R-134a, R-410A, ammonia, carbon dioxide.

figure.title: Vapour compression cycle
figure.aria: Four blocks in a loop: compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator, with the expansion valve marked as the constant enthalpy step.

chapters.example: A vapour compression refrigerator using R-134a works between an evaporating temperature of -10 °C and a condensing temperature of 40 °C. The table gives h1 = 395.0, h2 = 435.0, h3 = h4 = 250.0 kJ/kg. Find the refrigeration effect, the compressor work, the COP, the Carnot COP and the mass flow for 1 tonne of refrigeration. Answer: effect = 395.0 - 250.0 = 145.0 kJ/kg; work = 435.0 - 395.0 = 40.0 kJ/kg; COP = 145.0/40.0 = 3.63. Carnot COP = 263.15/(313.15 - 263.15) = 263.15/50 = 5.26. For 3.5 kW, mass flow = 3.5/145.0 = 0.024 kg/s.
chapters.trap: Drawing the expansion as isentropic on the T-s diagram, or using h3 - h4 as work. The throttle produces no work; the only work is h2 - h1.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 6.5 and 6.6 (Rankine and its T-s shape); Unit 5 (property tables).
chapters.leave: Refrigerant nomenclature, ozone and global warming indices to the refrigeration course; psychrometry to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Replace the compressor with a heat-driven pair: the refrigerant vapour is absorbed by a liquid, pumped as a liquid, and boiled out again in the generator.
chapters.depth: Components: generator (heat input), condenser, expansion valve, evaporator, absorber, solution pump, and usually a solution heat exchanger. Trace the two loops, refrigerant and solution. Pairs: ammonia-water, where ammonia is the refrigerant and water the absorbent; lithium bromide-water, where water is the refrigerant and LiBr the absorbent. COP = Q_E/(Q_G + W_p) — the generator heat replaces the compressor work, which is why the COP is defined on a different base. Explain why this suits waste heat, solar heat and places without reliable electricity: almost no moving parts and only a small pump. State that the COP is below 1, usually about 0.5 to 0.7 for a single-effect LiBr-water unit, against 3 to 5 for a vapour compression machine, and that the trade is cheap heat for low COP.

figure.title: Vapour absorption cycle
figure.aria: A loop of generator, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator, absorber and pump, with dashed solution lines returning from the generator to the absorber.

chapters.example: A vapour absorption chiller produces 100 kW of cooling from 150 kW of generator heat and 2 kW of pump work. Find the COP and the heat rejected in the condenser and absorber together. Answer: COP = Q_E/(Q_G + W_p) = 100/(150 + 2) = 0.658. Energy balance: Q_E + Q_G + W_p = 100 + 150 + 2 = 252 kW, so the condenser and absorber together reject 252 kW.
chapters.trap: Putting compressor work in the denominator, or using the Carnot COP formula. Also naming the wrong fluid as the refrigerant: in the LiBr-water pair the refrigerant is water, not the salt.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.7 (vapour compression cycle and COP); Unit 2 (energy balance on a steady flow device).
chapters.leave: Solution concentration charts, crystallisation limits and multi-effect machines to the refrigeration elective.
